values.value: Why a shared language between AI and your tools is such a powerful idea.
Four USB connectors arranged against a grey background
Photo by Hal Gatewood on Unsplash

value.markup:
There is a familiar moment in almost every useful AI conversation: the idea is clear, but the work is somewhere else. The content lives in a CMS. The image sits in a folder. The structure exists behind an API. Getting between those places can take more effort than the idea itself.

A connection worth getting excited about

Model Context Protocol gives AI applications a common way to connect to servers that expose capabilities. Tools describe actions an application can call; resources supply context; prompts provide reusable interaction templates. That shared vocabulary makes it possible to discover what a server offers instead of treating every integration as an entirely separate conversation. The official MCP architecture overview explains these building blocks.

To me, the exciting part is what that makes possible in everyday work. Imagine asking for a blog and having the next step be an inspection of the actual CMS: its existing types, its editors, its content tree. The conversation now has something concrete to work with.

Less translation, more making

This journal is a small example. Through the local Umbraco MCP server, we created page types, configured a block grid, imported supplied photographs, and published content. Those are separate CMS operations, but they belong to one understandable task: make a place for two stories.

My favourite benefit is continuity. A heading can travel from an idea into an editable content field, while the page structure stays recognisable to an Umbraco editor. The result is something a person can inspect and revise in the backoffice.

The useful kind of awesome

A protocol does not make every decision correct. Good naming, clear content models, and checking the saved result still matter. In fact, a connection to real tools makes those habits more valuable: there is now a real result to check.

That is why MCP feels promising. It brings the conversation closer to the work. Fewer disconnected handoffs, more tangible progress, and more room to spend attention on the thing you wanted to make in the first place.

values.value: A little Umbraco experiment with a big payoff: ideas become editable, structured content.
Colourful source code displayed on a dark computer screen
Photo by Chris Ried on Unsplash

value.markup:
A good demo should leave something useful behind. For this experiment, the brief was simple: create a blog front page, write two posts about MCP, and use the local Umbraco server to make it happen. The interesting part is how many ordinary CMS tasks fit into that small request.

Start with the shape of the content

Before writing a view, we inspected the project conventions and the existing CMS. The published WWW repository was already there. We added a front page beneath it and a post type for its children, keeping the new types in the Pages folder.

Then came three reusable blocks: a hero for the introduction and photograph, rich text for the story, and a listing for the published posts. Each page stores its main content in a block grid. That gives an editor a familiar place to change the words or rearrange the page.

Make the CMS do the CMS work

The MCP tools created the schema and content through Umbraco. They also imported two photographs from the project's Unsplash collection into a named media folder. There was no need to invent an alternative content store or write a migration to insert the articles.

Reading the pages back was a particularly satisfying checkpoint. We could verify the published state, the block keys, and the image selections against what Umbraco had actually saved. A successful write is useful; seeing the saved result makes it much easier to trust the next step.

Keep the rendering conventions

Content modeling and rendering still have different jobs. Once the content was ready, the site needed a rebuild and restart so its generated models could catch up. The Razor pages then used Umbraco's standard block renderer, with each block mapped to a plain model and rendered by a ViewComponent.

That boundary is a strength of the experiment. MCP handled the CMS operations, and the application kept its established rendering pipeline. An editor gets structured content, while a developer gets components with a clear responsibility.

Small demo, practical possibility

What makes MCP awesome here is the short path from intention to something editable. The outcome is a real content tree, real media, and two published stories. The next change can begin from that existing structure. For a modest local experiment, that is a very useful place to end up.
